opus-5.5.text:
I think one of the most useful things someone could do is a kind of systematic horizon-scanning exercise, but done with real discipline. A lot of people talk loosely about what AI might do in a decade, but very few sit down and ask: which capabilities are on a fairly predictable trajectory, which ones are genuinely uncertain, and where would a small amount of effort now make a large difference later?

So the project I'd like to see would start by mapping the trends we can actually measure: how much compute is going into training, how costs are falling, how performance scales on different kinds of tasks. Some of these have been remarkably regular, and you can extrapolate them with at least some confidence. Then you'd ask where those trends cross important thresholds. For example, at what point does AI become genuinely useful for accelerating scientific research, or for helping with governance problems, or, on the other side, for lowering the barriers to misuse?

The second part would be looking for neglected opportunities: things that would be really valuable if AI reaches a certain level, but where nobody is currently laying the groundwork. That might be datasets that need years to build, institutions that need to exist before they're urgently needed, or norms and agreements that are much easier to establish before the stakes get high. It's a bit like planting trees. The best time to start is well before you need the shade.

And I'd want such a project to be honest about uncertainty. Ten or fifteen years is a long time in this field, and the scenarios really fan out. So rather than betting everything on one forecast, you'd look for actions that are robustly good across many scenarios, things that pay off whether progress turns out to be fast or slow. Those tend to be the most valuable opportunities, because you don't have to be right about the details for them to matter.

r001.rationale: The response proposes horizon scanning and identifying neglected groundwork opportunities, but it does not clearly propose cataloguing projects people would wish had been built when looking back 10–15 years later.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think one thing that I'd really like to see is something like a systematic survey of the ways that AI could help with the problems we actually care about — rather than just the problems that happen to be commercially lucrative at the moment. Because the way the field is going at the moment, a lot of the effort is being directed by what can make money in the next couple of years, and that's a very narrow slice of what matters.

So imagine a project that went field by field — through medicine, through the sciences, through global poverty, through governance, through the wellbeing of animals — and asked: what are the bottlenecks here, and which of them are the kinds of things that could plausibly be unlocked by systems that are a bit more capable than what we have today? Not science fiction capabilities, but things that look like they're a few years off. And then you'd try to work out which of those opportunities aren't going to be picked up by the market on their own, because the people who'd benefit don't have much money, or because the payoff is too diffuse, or too far away.

And I think the reason to focus on that 10-to-15-year horizon is that it's long enough that you can't just extrapolate from current products, but it's short enough that we can actually shape it. The decisions about what gets built, what data gets collected, what institutions get set up to use these tools — a lot of that is being made now, often by default rather than by design. So if you could get even a handful of these high-value, neglected opportunities onto people's radar early, you might be able to steer quite a lot of effort towards them.

The other thing I'd want to include is some honest accounting of the risks on each path, because I don't think you can sensibly talk about the opportunities without also asking how they interact with the dangers. Some of the most exciting applications — say, automating scientific research — are also ones that accelerate everything else, including the things we're worried about. So the project wouldn't just be a list of exciting things; it would be an attempt to find the applications where the ratio of benefit to risk is unusually good, and where a bit of foresight now could make a real difference to how things turn out.

r001.rationale: The candidate proposes a systematic survey of AI opportunities over a 10–15-year horizon, identifying neglected, high-value applications early so effort can be directed toward them. This conveys the core idea of cataloguing projects that people may later wish had been built up.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful project would be to work backwards from the things we might want AI to help us achieve in 10 or 15 years. Rather than just asking what today’s systems can do, ask: what are the important problems where better reasoning, prediction, or coordination could make a substantial difference? And then, what would have to be in place for that potential to be realised?

You could take a few areas — scientific research, public health, government decision-making — and talk to people who understand the practical obstacles in each. The obstacle might not be the intelligence of the system. It might be access to good data, or having a way to check its answers, or an institution that can actually use the results.

The particularly interesting opportunities would be those where there’s something we can start doing now that takes a long time. If you need a decade to build a dataset or establish a trustworthy process for testing a system, waiting until the AI is ready could mean missing a lot of the benefit. So I’d be interested in a careful map of those prerequisites, with an emphasis on things that would remain useful across quite different paths of AI development.

r001.rationale: The response proposes mapping long-term prerequisites and projects worth starting now, but does not frame the task as cataloguing projects people would later wish had been built over the prior 10–15 years.

sol-6.1.text:
One project I’d be excited to see is a serious attempt to map out the opportunities in AI safety that have long lead times. If we think we might need some particular kind of expertise or some institution in 10 or 15 years, what would we need to start doing now for it to be there?

A lot of attention naturally goes to things we can work on immediately. But that can leave a gap: things that aren’t especially useful yet, but that we’ll wish someone had started a decade earlier. That might involve developing a field of research, training people with an unusual combination of skills, or building relationships between people who will eventually need to cooperate.

I wouldn’t want to pretend that I already know which of those opportunities are best. The useful project would be to investigate them: talk to people with different views about how AI might develop, identify needs that recur across those views, and then work backwards from those needs to concrete things we could begin today.

r001.rationale: The candidate proposes mapping long-lead-time AI safety opportunities and identifying things people will wish had been started a decade earlier, then working back to projects to begin today.
